content: Vibrio cholerae is a gram-negative bacterium with a curved rod shape that is responsible for causing cholera in humans. It belongs to the gamma subdivision of the Proteobacteria and is part of the genus Vibrio. There are two primary strains of Vibrio cholerae, known as the classic and El Tor strains, along with numerous other serogroups. The bacterium was first identified as the causative agent of cholera by Italian anatomist Filippo Pacini in 1854. However, his discovery did not gain widespread recognition until Robert Koch independently publicized the findings and methods to combat the disease approximately 30 years later. Vibrio cholerae naturally inhabits aquatic environments, including fresh, brackish, and saltwater ecosystems. It is primarily associated with copepods in the zooplankton community. Cholera outbreaks in coastal regions are often linked to zooplankton blooms, making cholera a typical example of a zoonotic disease. The pathogenesis of Vibrio cholerae involves colonization of the gastrointestinal tract, where the bacterium adheres to villous absorptive cells using pili. It secretes a binary toxin known as cholera toxin (CT), which consists of two subunits, A and B, synthesized in a 1:5 ratio. The B subunits bind to host cells and facilitate the internalization of the A subunit, which is subsequently processed into its active A1 form. The A1 subunit catalyzes ADP-ribosylation of the regulatory component of adenylate cyclase, activating the enzyme. This activation leads to increased cyclic AMP (cAMP) production, resulting in massive fluid and electrolyte loss from the intestinal cells, which manifests as severe diarrhea. The genes encoding cholera toxin, ctxAB, are located on a specific filamentous bacteriophage. The transduction of this phage depends on the bacterial expression of the Toxin Coregulated Pilus (TCP), which is encoded by the Vibrio cholerae pathogenicity island (VPI). VPI is typically present only in virulent strains and is laterally transferred between bacteria. Initially, VPI was thought to encode a filamentous phage responsible for its transfer, but this theory was disproven by a study of 46 diverse Vibrio cholerae isolates, which found no evidence of VPI phage production. Instead, the generalized transduction phage CP-T1 has been shown to transduce the entire VPI, which is then integrated into the same chromosomal location. Additionally, VPI can excise and circularize to form pVPI through a specialized mechanism involving VPI-encoded recombinases. It remains unclear whether pVPI plays a role in CP-T1 transduction or if it is part of an alternative VPI mobilization mechanism. Vibrio cholerae also produces two proteases, chitinase and mucinase. Chitinase enables the bacterium to colonize copepods, while mucinase, a non-specific protease, facilitates entry into the human gastrointestinal tract. Furthermore, Vibrio cholerae produces a toxin called ZOT (Zona Occludens Toxin), which specifically targets the tight junctions (zona occludens) that connect epithelial cells. In terms of differential diagnosis, Vibrio cholerae infection must be distinguished from other causes of viral, bacterial, and parasitic gastroenteritis. Small bowel diarrhea caused by Vibrio cholerae is typically watery and voluminous, with fewer than 5 white blood cells (WBCs) per high-power field. In contrast, large bowel diarrhea is characterized by mucous or bloody stools, lower volume, and more than 10 WBCs per high-power field. The WBC count in stool can vary significantly, potentially reaching as high as 1000, depending on the patient’s immune system response.
